ai.definition: Synthetic Consciousness is a theoretical approach that aims to create artificial systems capable of experiencing or simulating conscious states, leveraging advances in neuromorphic computing.
ai.howItWorks: Theoretical models and simulations are used to replicate brain functions at the neural network level. This involves creating complex algorithms and hardware architectures designed to mimic the behavior of biological neurons and synapses, with the goal of achieving a state that can be interpreted as conscious experience.
ai.problemSolved: Understanding the fundamental nature of consciousness and potentially developing technologies for artificial intelligence with human-like awareness or sentience.
ai.manufacturing: Currently theoretical; no specific manufacturing processes have been developed. Requires advanced neuromorphic hardware design and materials science to create scalable, energy-efficient devices that can simulate large-scale neural networks.
ai.buildProcess: Involves designing and simulating artificial neural networks on supercomputers or specialized neuromorphic hardware. Theoretical models are iteratively refined through simulations and experiments to better mimic biological systems.
ai.costDrivers: High computational resources, advanced materials for neuromorphic hardware, and extensive research and development costs. Current estimates suggest that significant investment is required before practical applications can be developed.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Theoretical and speculative at this stage; potential future application in AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science remains uncertain but highly intriguing.
ai.regulation: No specific regulatory framework exists for synthetic consciousness research. However, as the technology matures, ethical considerations related to artificial sentience may prompt new regulations.
ai.risks: Ethical concerns about creating sentient entities, potential misuse of technology, and unknown long-term effects on human society and AI development.
ai.profitability: Uncertain; current focus is on scientific understanding rather than commercial applications. Potential future benefits could lead to significant economic impact in healthcare, robotics, and other fields if successful.
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected advancements in neuromorphic hardware, increased computational power, and better understanding of the neural basis of consciousness will drive further research and development.
ai.energyRequirements: High for large-scale simulations; field units draw low hundreds of watts. Fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and other specialized processes required for neuromorphic materials.

glossary.def: A type of computing inspired by the structure and function of biological neural systems, often used to simulate complex neural networks.
Theoretical models for creating artificial systems capable of experiencing or simulating conscious states through advanced computational techniques.

subsystems.name: Neuromorphic substrate
subsystems.role: hardware that mimics neurons and synapses in their own physics rather than simulating them as arithmetic.

subsystems.name: Neural model
subsystems.role: the equations and cell types that decide how activity propagates.

subsystems.name: Connectome data pipeline
subsystems.role: the wiring diagram the model is built from.

subsystems.name: Embodiment and sensors
subsystems.role: gives the model a world to act in, so its internal states have causes.

subsystems.name: Measurement and theory
subsystems.role: criteria for judging whether a system is conscious, and instruments to test them.
parts: brain-activity recording (electrodes, calcium imaging, fMRI, EEG)

subsystems.name: Compute and power
subsystems.role: energy and silicon to run large models continuously.

buildSteps.title: Map a nervous system
buildSteps.detail: Slice tissue into nanometre-thin sections, image them, and trace every neuron and synapse by machine plus human proofreading. This has been completed only for small organisms such as the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, with around 300 neurons; partial maps exist for larger brains.

buildSteps.title: Build a simulation of it
buildSteps.detail: Turn the wiring diagram into a spiking network on GPUs or neuromorphic chips, choosing how detailed each neuron and synapse must be.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop through a body
buildSteps.detail: Connect the model to sensors and a simulated or robotic body so it receives input and its outputs change that input — models of small animals driving virtual bodies are the current benchmark.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate against real brains
buildSteps.detail: Compare the model's activity with recordings from the living organism and adjust cell properties and connection strengths until statistics match.

buildSteps.title: Add the architecture theories point to
buildSteps.detail: Introduce the features implicated in conscious processing — dense recurrent loops, a global broadcast-like pathway, thalamocortical-style feedback — rather than a purely feed-forward network.

buildSteps.title: Test for markers, not behaviour
buildSteps.detail: Apply measures such as perturbational complexity, which probes how rich and irreducible a system's response to a stimulus is, and check whether the model reproduces human-like signatures.

buildSteps.title: Scale and iterate
buildSteps.detail: Extend from insect-scale to mammalian cortex, keeping the model embodied and continuously checked against new recordings.

prerequisites.why: complete maps exist only for very small nervous systems; human-scale mapping is far beyond current imaging and proofreading throughput.
research chips such as Intel's Loihi and Manchester's SpiNNaker show the principle, but no machine yet approaches a human brain's ~86 billion neurons.
theories such as integrated information theory and global workspace theory make different predictions and are being compared in adversarial human experiments; none is settled.
electrodes and imaging reach limited numbers of neurons at once, so there is no full reference recording to validate a large model against.
a human brain runs on roughly 20 watts; simulating one on conventional supercomputers needs megawatts.

pathway.milestone: connectomes and closed-loop whole-brain models of insects and small vertebrates; consciousness theories tested in humans with brain stimulation and imaging
pathway.unlocks: a data-driven loop between theory, measurement and simulation.

pathway.milestone: embodied models of a small mammal brain running in real time on neuromorphic hardware
pathway.unlocks: testing whether biological-scale dynamics can be reproduced in silicon at practical power.

pathway.milestone: mammalian-cortical-scale models that learn and match living recordings
pathway.unlocks: a candidate substrate on which consciousness markers could be measured, if any apply.

pathway.milestone: an agreed, validated test for machine consciousness
pathway.unlocks: only then could anyone say whether a synthetic system is conscious — currently there is no such test, and it is an open question whether consciousness depends on biological tissue at all.
